lines: אֵין לָנוּ זוּלָתְךָ, אֵל שְׁלֵם בְּמִדּוֹת

review: The hymn is the assembly's greeting: 1:1–2 is the smile of the Lord healing (Prov 15:30, מְאוֹר־עֵינַיִם יְשַׂמַּח־לֵב) with Num 6:26, 2:1–4 is Ps 133:1 (מַה־טּוֹב וּמַה־נָּעִים שֶׁבֶת אַחִים גַּם־יָחַד) with Col 3:16, and 3:1–4 is Ps 16:2 with Phil 4:19 and Eph 3:16.

The shape is 2/4/4: stanza 1 is a two-line acclamation and stanzas 2–3 have four long lines each. The payload keeps stanza 1 at two lines, because the printed book sets it as a couplet before the hymn proper begins.

1:1 שְׂפָתְךָ הַשְּׂחוֹק — the Arabic ثَغْرُكَ الْبَسَّام is literally 'your smiling mouth'; Hebrew has no adjective from the root of שָׂחַק that will sit in a construct, so the line uses the noun הַשְּׂחוֹק with שְׂפָתֶיךָ as the subject, keeping the smile on the lips rather than on the face.

2:3 מַה־נָּעִים אַחִים בְּיַחַד — the Arabic مَا أَجْمَلَ الْإِخْوَان is 'how fair the brethren'; the Hebrew quotes Ps 133:1's מַה־נָּעִים … גַּם־יָחַד and keeps אַחִים, so the stanza's fellowship is the psalm's and not a general sociability.

3:2 אֵל הַמַּתָּנוֹת — the Arabic يَا مَانِحَ الْهِبَات is 'O Giver of gifts'; the Hebrew keeps the construct with the plural מַתָּנוֹת (the word of Jas 1:17, מַתְּנֵי טוֹב), because the stanza is listing what God gives and the singular would flatten it into a title.
